item.title: Rise of domestic brands reeling in 'China haul'
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
Rise of domestic brands reeling in 'China haul' Mariana Rizzo, a 23-year-old Italian studying architecture at the University of Naples Federico II, has made shopping part of her experience of everyday life in China. She first visited the country in 2023 and has returned three times, with some trips lasting almost two months. Her shopping list includes beauty products, clothing, accessories, snacks, technology and lifestyle goods, as well as items that are harder to find in Italy. "When it comes to Chinese brands, one of the beauty brands I really like is Flower Knows. I love their makeup, but also the packaging and the attention they put into the design," she said. Rizzo is among the growing number of foreigners visiting the country for the "China haul" — a trend of international travelers filling their suitcases with Chinese products before heading home. Underpinning the phenomenon is the growing appreciation of the quality and modern appeal of Chinese brands often highlighted on social media and shopping platforms. "Sometimes I see something on Xiaohongshu or Douyin and think, 'I need to find this when I go to China!'" Rizzo said. "For me, shopping in China is not just about getting something cheaper. It's about having access to a much wider variety of products and experiencing the trends and lifestyle of the country directly," she said. Her favorite purchases include a qipao, the traditional dress worn by Chinese women, and a DJI Osmo Pocket 4 camera for recording her travels. "Buying it in China was particularly interesting because DJI is a Chinese technology brand, and I was able to discover and buy it directly there," said Rizzo, adding that the camera was considerably cheaper in China than in Italy. She has also noticed growing interest in Chinese products and brands among her friends and classmates in Italy, and sometimes she introduces them to brands she has discovered. A US tourist is measured for a custom-made suit at a clothing store in the South Bund Fabric Market in Shanghai on July 22. WANG XIANG/XINHUA Better than socks The appeal of homegrown Chinese brands among overseas shoppers is increasingly visible in Shanghai. Foreign customers accounted for about 35 percent of sales at footwear brand Pane's two Shanghai stores, while overseas shoppers accounted for around 30 percent of sales at Wangxiaoben's Shanghai stores, according to a report by Jiefang Daily in June. Wang Xianming, founder of Wangxiaoben, a Chinese lifestyle brand known for its bags, said the appeal lies in the happiness their products bring shoppers. When he established the brand in 2016, he started with socks, hoping to turn a basic necessity into an accessory that could lift people's mood. "I wanted socks to be more than just something people wear. They could also complement an outfit, express a sense of style and bring a little happiness to everyday life, even if only for 15 seconds," Wang said. In 2024, Wangxiaoben began making what Wang calls "dopamine" bags, which have since become its main product category. The brand's product range also includes hats, socks and pet accessories. Wang first noticed an increase in foreign customers in 2024, particularly visitors from Southeast Asia and Russia shopping at the company's store in Shanghai's Super Brand Mall. In September 2025 it opened a store at Shanghai Joy City and noticed South Korean and American bloggers sharing content about its products. "Online platforms in Thailand and Russia began working with us, making our products available to new consumers," said Wang of the overseas bloggers' brand promotions. One South Korean blogger, for example, posted a video of the brand's Shanghai store this summer, prompting numerous inquiries from her followers. She subsequently bought more than 100 bags for followers and friends during her stay in the city. Wangxiaoben products have also attracted repeat international shoppers. A Malaysian woman visited Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, three times over two years, buying multiple products on each trip and developing a close friendship with the store manager, Wang said. Customers from Southeast Asia tend to prefer lower-priced bags, while those from Japan and South Korea seem to care less about prices. The brand's overseas customers also span a wider age range than its younger Chinese shoppers. "We are not making major adjustments specifically for foreign customers. In Shanghai, we are looking into tax-refund policies and other measures to make shopping more convenient for international visitors," Wang said. Wangxiaoben has around 120 stores nationwide, mainly in tourist destinations and major cities such as Shanghai, Hangzhou, Nanjing in Jiangsu province, and Chengdu in Sichuan province. It has registered its trademarks overseas and plans to expand gradually into international markets through social media promotion, while exploring complementary products around the lifestyle concept behind its "dopamine" range. "I can clearly see that overseas consumers are developing greater trust in and appreciation for Chinese brands. This is closely related to the development of China's manufacturing, design and branding capabilities. It feels a little like how Chinese consumers once felt when they went abroad to buy local brands," said Wang. Premium goods Beyond individual shopping experiences, broader consumer perceptions of Chinese brands are evolving. According to Ipsos' 2025 Global Trust Index for Chinese Brands, the global net trust score for Chinese brands rose by 12 percentage points from the previous year to 32 percent, while the proportion of consumers in developed markets who expressed trust in Chinese brands reached 36 percent. Guo Xiaoling, a professor of marketing at the Business School of the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, said Chinese brands must win acceptance, trust and even become aspirational for consumers in developed markets to command a price premium. "In the early 2000s, when China joined the World Trade Organization, 'Made in China' was often associated with low prices and value for money, targeting lower-end market segments rather than mainstream markets. Over the past two decades, China has made significant progress in the transition from Chinese products to Chinese brands," said Guo. Overseas perceptions of Chinese brands have been shaped by China's growing national strength and cultural influence, breakthroughs in artificial intelligence and new energy vehicles, as well as improvements in innovation, design, quality and sustainability, she said. Citing Bain & Company's 2025 China Personal Luxury Report, Guo pointed to homegrown high-end brands such as fashion label Icicle, jewelry brand Laopu Gold, fragrance brand Documents and handbag maker Songmont. "Brand craftsmanship, storytelling and interactions with potential consumers on social media now play a major role in stimulating consumer interest and desire," said Guo. At Songmont's flagship store at Indigo shopping mall in Beijing, she met young foreign consumers who had come specifically to shop and learned they had discovered the brand through social media. When teaching foreign exchange students, Guo asked them to visit well-known Chinese brand experience spaces, such as Pop Land. She believes these firsthand interactions deepen their understanding of Chinese brands and culture and encourage positive word-of-mouth when they return home. "If social media is the digital infrastructure for elevating Chinese brands, then firsthand experience is the booster and the experience capsule built on top of it," she said. Chinese businesses should recognize that their brands represent the country to overseas consumers, whether through Laopu Gold's cultural heritage or Pop Mart's broader appeal. "When overseas consumers learn that a brand they like originates in China, their fondness for that brand will inevitably lead to a more positive perception of Chinese brands as a whole," said Guo. A livestream host for a cross-border e-commerce platform showcases new jewelry collections at the Yiwu Global Digital Trade Center in Yiwu, Zhejiang province, ahead of this year's Singles Day shopping rush. LYU BIN/FOR CHINA DAILY Cross-border sales While overseas consumers are increasingly discovering Chinese products through travel and social media, Chinese e-commerce platforms are also stepping up efforts to reach them in their home markets. China's cross-border e-commerce imports and exports reached 2.84 trillion yuan in 2025, up 4.8 percent year-on-year, the General Administration of Customs said at a press conference in July. The challenge for Chinese businesses is turning overseas consumer interest into purchases and repeat business, with this year's overseas Singles Day shopping season already underway. AliExpress launched its sales campaign on Nov 1, with promotions running through Nov 18 before moving into its Black Friday campaign. According to AliExpress data, the volume of goods stocked in its overseas warehouses ahead of this year's Singles Day online shopping rush rose 146 percent year-on-year. George Wang, chief financial officer of Shoplazza, an AI-native e-commerce platform that has served more than 650,000 merchants worldwide, said merchants' priorities have shifted from simply setting up overseas online stores to learning how to operate and grow their businesses in international markets. "Acquiring customers online has become harder, so merchants have to watch spending, conversion and margins much more closely. Over the past two years, one clear trend is that merchants' needs are shifting from 'help me set up an overseas online store' to 'help me run my overseas business'," said Wang. "Social media helps consumers discover brands, and this sparks their interest, while content creators build trust through product reviews, demonstrations, and firsthand experiences," he said. Overseas consumers usually pass through several processes before buying, including watching a product video on social media, reading a creator's review, and comparing options on a marketplace or the brand's own website. "Some brands using Shoplazza's platform include links on their online stores that direct customers to Amazon, allowing consumers to choose their preferred purchasing channel. This approach lets the two channels work together, with the brand's own online store driving traffic to Amazon while helping merchants build lasting customer relationships through direct sales," said Wang. On Oct 5, TikTok announced an AI shopping assistant and Buy Direct, a one-click checkout tool, with partners including Shoplazza. "The shopping assistant allows consumers to ask about sizing, product details, delivery and stock before proceeding to the checkout, without leaving the TikTok app," he said. Wang gave the example of Real-SilkLife, a Chinese direct-to-consumer brand offering silk, cashmere and linen clothing and home products, primarily in the US and Europe. By using Shoplazza's system and AI agents to streamline tasks such as store setup, product listing, multilingual content management and data analysis, the brand increased regional orders by 30 percent and average order value by 22 percent over three months. Wang said another example is JammyJem, a Chinese brand selling squishy toys and blind-box products. "It uses online livestreams and TikTok short videos to engage overseas consumers, and buyers also share their purchases and unboxing videos, drawing in new shoppers," he said. JammyJem's data for Japan showed that around 60 percent of its customers who placed orders in a given month made at least two purchases that month, while about one-third placed orders five or more times. Rizzo, the Italian student, said her interest in Chinese products continues after she returns to Italy. She typically selects items on Taobao, Tmall and JD.com before traveling and has them delivered to an address in China. She tried ordering from China to Italy once but found international shipping expensive, particularly when buying from multiple sellers. Charl Albertyn is a 34-year-old South African who has lived in China since 2014. Through his company, Hofmeyr Consulting, he organizes trips for international visitors, while his work with Lumiverse Media LLC focuses on Chinese business, technology, food and consumer culture. Albertyn said his perception of Chinese brands had changed considerably over the years. He has witnessed Chinese companies grow stronger, not only in manufacturing, but also in design, technology, branding and consumer experience. "I don't think price is necessarily the most important attraction anymore," he said. "Chinese products can be attractive because of their quality, design, variety and technological innovation, but perhaps most importantly because they increasingly offer something that is distinctly Chinese." He sees this as part of a broader shift in China's global image. "After living here for more than a decade, that is probably the biggest change I have seen: China has moved from being perceived primarily as the world's factory to increasingly being recognized as a source of brands, products, experiences and ideas in its own right," said Albertyn. item.title: Global South delegates seek stronger voice at World Media Summit in Beijing
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
Global South delegates seek stronger voice at World Media Summit in Beijing BEIJING, Nov. 8 (Xinhua) -- Senior media professionals from the Global South have called for closer cooperation at the 7th World Media Summit in Beijing to give their countries a stronger voice in global coverage as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes the industry. Co-organized by Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing municipal government, this year's summit runs from Nov. 5 to 9. It has drawn nearly 500 representatives of media outlets, think tanks and government bodies from 112 countries and regions, as well as the United Nations and other international organizations. Initiated in 2009, the World Media Summit has become a major platform for exchange and cooperation among media leaders and professionals across regions and language communities. "What is important about the summit is that it brings media outlets from around the world and gives us a forum to discuss the future of our industry," said Kenedid Ibrahim Houssein, director of publication of La Nation in Djibouti, who is attending the summit for the first time. "We hope to further develop partnership with China on information sharing based on this platform," he added. Ghislain Ruffin Etoughet Nzuet, chairman of the board of directors at Gabon Broadcasting Corporation, said the World Media Summit provides a platform for African countries to tell their own stories and speak for themselves. "Africa has a long tradition and a long history, yet very little is known about us," Nzuet said, adding that cooperation with partners around the world, particularly China, could help bring African perspectives into global discussions. Agnes Kalekye Nguna, managing director and CEO of Kenya Broadcasting Corporation, stressed the importance of dialogue among civilizations on an equal footing. She called for more initiatives to expand exchanges and deepen media cooperation between Africa and China, saying a partnership that benefits both sides could inspire similar efforts elsewhere in the Global South and beyond. Under this year's theme, "Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action," delegates are also discussing how Global South countries could work together to help their media organizations adapt as AI use expands across the industry. "How do we ensure smaller nations have a meaningful voice in shaping the future of AI?" asked Aminath Namza, chairperson of Public Service Media in the Maldives, during discussions at the summit. She said many AI models are trained on data drawn mainly from societies with a greater digital presence, and therefore may not be able to fully reflect the languages, cultures and realities of smaller nations. "International cooperation must therefore ensure that developing countries and small island states can contribute not only to AI's development, but also to the principles governing it," she said. On Saturday, the 7th World Media Summit released the Global Media Initiative for the Joint Development of AI Application Standards. Launched by Xinhua, the initiative brings together major media outlets and other professional organizations to safeguard the authenticity of information, protect data security, and uphold media ethics, thereby maintaining public trust in the media. Under this initiative, participants plan to work together for about two years to develop a set of standards that address different media uses of AI and are validated by media outlets. Najeh Missaoui, director general and CEO of Tunis Afrique Presse, one of the first participants, regards the initiative as a major step forward. "It takes us from talking about AI to taking joint action and setting rules." "For us at Tunis Afrique Presse, this plan ensures that the Global South will have a hand in shaping the rules for AI, rather than simply consuming technology developed by others," he said. "We hope the initiative will become a practical avenue for cooperation, sharing expertise and building capacity, and media organizations of different sizes and with different resources can apply the standards," said Mohammed Alyami, director general of the Union of News Agencies of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, which is also among the first participants, in an interview with Xinhua. Wong Chun Wai, chairman of the Malaysian National News Agency (Bernama), said that, instead of access to basic AI tools, media organizations need to invest in advanced tools and train staff to use them effectively. He called on Global South countries to work together more closely in the changing media landscape and ensure that media organizations worldwide can share in the benefits of AI. Adopted at the summit on Saturday, the 7th World Media Summit Beijing Consensus calls for joint efforts to advance the transformation and development of the global media industry in the AI era. It commits to advancing the inclusive and responsible application of AI in the media sector so that advances in AI benefit media organizations at all stages of development and in every country. "The future of global communication must be intelligent, but above all, inclusive," said Viasen Soobramoney, CEO of South Africa's Independent Media IOL and the African News Agency, during the summit. Soobramoney called for transparent, accountable and inclusive global AI governance to help prevent the technology from reinforcing inequalities that have long affected many Global South countries. Africa and China could deepen cooperation in AI-assisted translation, multimedia production, journalist training, content verification and the exchange of technical expertise, he said. Abdul Hakim, president director of Indonesia's Antara News Agency, suggested closer cooperation on information sharing and verification, more exchanges on responsible AI use and newsroom innovation, and better coordination in reporting on global challenges. "No country, no community, and no voice should be left behind," he said. "This is why international cooperation matters so much." Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Beyond market size, European firms tap China's growth, innovation potential
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-09
Beyond market size, European firms tap China's growth, innovation potential SHANGHAI, Nov. 8 (Xinhua) -- Amid dazzling displays at the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), a truck-sized turn-mill machine stands quietly, its computer-controlled spindle whirring. Without flashy decorations, the machine still draws curious crowds. The attraction is a piece of precision machinery from an Austrian "hidden champion" WFL, shown under the expo's "deep-tech" label. Weighing over 20 tonnes, the machine began its journey in August, crossing oceans and moving between trucks and shipping containers before arriving at the Port of Shanghai, host city of the CIIE -- a major platform for China to open its vast market to the world. Why go to such lengths? Mayr Günther Franz Josef, general manager of WFL, told Xinhua that participating in the CIIE offers a chance to gain firsthand insights into China's rapidly upgrading high-end manufacturing sector and to forge closer ties with industrial partners across the Asia-Pacific region. The company had another goal in mind: to make the machine's journey a one-way trip. As hoped, it found a buyer just three days into the expo. Across the exhibition floor, European companies are deepening their engagement with China, drawn not only by the sheer size of its market but increasingly by opportunities arising from industrial upgrading, evolving consumer demand and a vibrant innovation ecosystem. MORE THAN A VAST MARKET China's pursuit of high-quality development, coupled with rising living standards, has fueled increasingly sophisticated demand for industrial and consumer products, opening up new avenues of growth for businesses worldwide. "As China's manufacturing capabilities continue to advance, demand for high-end machine tools and other sophisticated industrial equipment is growing," said Zheng Xiaoli, a representative at WFL's booth. The company's machine tools are used to manufacture complex, high-precision components for industries including aviation, aerospace and shipbuilding. The changing composition of their Chinese clientele offers a glimpse into that transformation. "Our customers in China used to be mainly state-owned enterprises and foreign-invested companies. Now, a growing number of private Chinese manufacturers seeking quality products are investing in our high-end machinery," said Zheng. China's accelerating green transition and digital transformation are also creating fresh opportunities for European suppliers of advanced technologies and specialized materials. For AMORNEX, a joint venture between Luxembourg-based steelmaker ArcelorMittal and China Oriental Group, the booming electric vehicle industry in China is driving demand for advanced materials. Jurgen Cobbaut, the company's chief marketing officer, told Xinhua that some high-performance electric motors in Chinese EVs require materials with exceptional strength and efficiency, which plays to the company's strengths. "It's not only the volume, but also the level of sophistication. That is what really makes it interesting," Cobbaut said of the Chinese market. The shift toward more sophisticated demand extends to consumer markets, where changing lifestyles and rising expectations are also inspiring product innovation. German cleaning equipment manufacturer Kärcher, for example, developed a compact, foldable pressure washer for cleaning bicycles, cars and camping gear, tapping into Chinese consumers' growing enthusiasm for outdoor activities. Originally designed for the Chinese market, the product has since been rolled out globally. "Chinese consumers today are much more sophisticated. They're looking for products that fit their lifestyles," said Bernd Rützler, an executive vice president of Alfred Kärcher GmbH & Co. KG. INNOVATION ENGINE Beyond evolving demand, China's innovation capabilities, underpinned by its extensive supply chains and fast-evolving market, are becoming powerful draws for European companies. "China has always been one of our most important strategic markets globally. What has changed is the increasingly multifaceted role China plays," said Liu Ling, chief region leader of Philips China. For the Dutch health technology company, China is not only its second-largest market worldwide but also a "key supply-chain hub and engine of innovation." Increasingly, innovations developed in China are also finding their way into European companies' global product portfolios. Drawing on China's "strong industrial foundation, abundant innovation resources and diverse use cases," Schneider Electric has worked with Chinese partners to develop a range of proven, scalable solutions that are helping businesses across sectors become smarter, more efficient and greener, said Yin Zheng, executive vice president of China & East Asia Operations of Schneider Electric. In the medical equipment hall at the CIIE, widely regarded as one of the expo's most competitive sections, Swedish medical equipment manufacturer Elekta is showcasing its AI-powered AutoART adaptive radiotherapy solution. The system can shorten the adaptive radiotherapy process -- from imaging and treatment planning to treatment delivery -- to just 10 to 15 minutes. Developed in response to the demands of China's busy radiotherapy departments, this technology is intended for wider international use, according to Jin Jianxue, vice president and medical affairs director of Elekta China. COMPLEMENTARY STRENGTHS The CIIE offers a timely view of deepening business ties between China and Europe, as EU policymakers weigh trade issues with China. The deeper ties are rooted in strong complementarity between the two sides, said Shen Yi, an international relations scholar at Fudan University. As China seeks to upgrade its industries and improve living standards, it needs European products and expertise in areas such as advanced equipment, precision instruments, pharmaceuticals and professional services, Shen told Xinhua. Europe, in turn, stands to benefit from China's vast market, manufacturing capabilities and technological advances in sectors like batteries and solar power, he added. Illustrating such complementarity, Zhang Shuo, chief representative at the Beijing Representative Office of the Brussels-based European Automobile Manufacturers Association (ACEA), noted that Europe's century-old automotive industry has deep expertise in engineering, safety and environmental technologies, while China has taken the lead in batteries and electric mobility. Cooperation is also moving beyond the traditional model of importing finished vehicles or transferring technology toward closer integration of industrial supply chains and joint research and development, he told Xinhua at their booth. ACEA is attending this year's CIIE as an exhibitor for the first time, although its member companies have long been regular participants. Going forward, China has called for an "upward balance" in trade, achieved through greater openness and an expanding economic pie, rather than a "downward balance" caused by closing markets. Ultimately, openness remains a powerful draw. As Rützler put it: "We see China as a reliable market and a reliable partner. Its continued opening up gives us the confidence to invest more." item.title: Chinese vice premier holds video call with U.S. treasury secretary, trade representative
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08
Chinese vice premier holds video call with U.S. treasury secretary, trade representative Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, also China's lead person for China-U.S. economic and trade affairs, holds a video call with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, on Nov. 6, 2026. (Xinhua/Tian Yu) BEIJING, Nov. 7 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, also China's lead person for China-U.S. economic and trade affairs, held a video call on Friday with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The two sides held candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on implementing the important consensus reached between the two heads of state at their meetings in Beijing and Washington and the outcomes of economic and trade consultations, and on key economic and trade issues of mutual concern. The Chinese side expressed serious concern over recent U.S. economic and trade restrictions against China. Both sides agreed that under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, they would further leverage the China-U.S. economic and trade consultation mechanism, continuously strengthen cooperation and properly manage differences so as to promote the stable and positive development of China-U.S. economic and trade relations, and contribute to building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity. item.title: From products to partnerships, CIIE sets stage for global debuts
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08
From products to partnerships, CIIE sets stage for global debuts People walk past an billboard themed on the ninth edition of the China International Import Expo (CIIE) at the National Exhibition and Convention Center (Shanghai) in east China's Shanghai, Nov. 5, 2026. The expo, the world's first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports, opened here on Thursday. Running from Nov. 5 to 10, this year's CIIE has attracted 4,142 overseas exhibitors, including more than 300 Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders. Total exhibition area exceeds 440,000 square meters this year. (Xinhua/Xing Guangli) SHANGHAI, Nov. 7 (Xinhua) -- For many global businesses, unveiling a new product or technology is more than showcasing innovation. It is also about reaching the right market. Austrian machine tool maker WFL Millturn Technologies knows this well. To make its Asian debut, the company's massive new machining center crossed continents and oceans, traveling for more than two months before arriving in Shanghai for this year's China International Import Expo (CIIE). "This visit to the CIIE will allow us to gain a close-up understanding of the development opportunities brought by the upgrading of China's high-end manufacturing industry," said Mayr Günther Franz Josef, WFL's general manager. A first-time participant at the expo, the company also hopes to deepen cooperation and strengthen ties with industrial partners across the Asia-Pacific region. WFL's journey speaks to the CIIE's appeal as a proven platform for global businesses to launch debuts and connect markets, innovation and industries. Now in its ninth edition, this year's CIIE is seeing more than 480 exhibits making their global, Asian or China debuts. The number sets a new record for the event, which has seen over 3,400 new products, technologies and services debut in the past eight editions. Many of them moved from the expo floor to store shelves and became bestsellers in the Chinese market. For French cosmetics giant L'Oréal, the CIIE is an ideal launchpad for new brands, new products, new innovations, and new partnerships. "Nearly half of our brands made their debut in the Chinese market through the CIIE," said Lan Zhenzhen, chief corporate affairs and engagement officer, L'Oréal North Asia & China. She added that these brands have since performed well in China. In China's five-year development blueprint for 2026-2030, the country has called for expanding imports and continuing to hold the CIIE and other major trade fairs, as well as actively promoting the "debut economy." "The Chinese market is a barometer for global product trends and innovation," said Xia Xianlin, account director at Joy Wing Mau Chile Spa. Introducing a new coconut product at the expo, the company hopes to leverage the CIIE's spillover effect to help more fruit products enter the Chinese market. At the CIIE, debuts do more than introduce new products. They spark further innovation as technologies and ideas from around the world meet local needs and partners. Danish pharmaceutical giant Novo Nordisk, which has participated in all the previous eight editions of the expo, is showcasing new medicines at this year's event, including Kyinsu, a once-weekly injection for type 2 diabetes. "The CIIE has become an important part of our work in China," said Mike Doustdar, president and CEO of Novo Nordisk. This is the company's ninth consecutive year at the CIIE, and many medicines first showcased at the expo have since reached the Chinese market. According to Novo Nordisk, Chinese experts have helped develop Kyinsu, serving as lead investigators in its global Phase III clinical trial and helping shape the global research. In telecommunications, U.S. tech company Qualcomm debuted the world's first 6G terminal prototype outside the laboratory. According to the company, the device has been used in 6G technology tests and validation conducted with its Chinese partners, including China Mobile and ZTE. "Qualcomm's participation in the CIIE is more than a number of visits. It reflects our journey of innovating and growing together with our Chinese partners," said Frank Meng, chairman of Qualcomm China. Unveiling a tire made with 75 percent renewable and recycled materials at the CIIE, French tire manufacturer Michelin has described its evolving approach to China as a shift from "In China, for China" to "With China, for the World." New trends and technologies in sectors ranging from electric vehicles to autonomous driving often emerge in China ahead of other markets, according to Jay Wu, Michelin China vice president, director of government relations and strategy. "China is both a test ground and a gym, a place where we test new ideas, challenge ourselves and continuously strengthen our innovation capabilities," Wu told Xinhua. item.title: China kicks off 43rd Antarctic scientific expedition
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08
China kicks off 43rd Antarctic scientific expedition Members of China's 43rd Antarctic scientific expedition team aboard the icebreaker Xuelong 2 are pictured before their departure from Nanshan Port in Sanya, south China's Hainan Province, Nov. 7, 2026. (Xinhua/Guo Cheng) SANYA, Nov. 7 (Xinhua) -- China held a departure ceremony in Sanya, south China's Hainan Province, on Saturday to mark the start of its 43rd Antarctic scientific expedition. Organized by the Ministry of Natural Resources, the mission will upgrade China's polar research stations and logistics network and carry out comprehensive multidisciplinary surveys and monitoring in Antarctica. It will also pursue priority research at the frontiers of polar science, test and apply domestically developed equipment, and deepen bilateral and multilateral cooperation in science and logistics support. The expedition is supported by the icebreakers Xuelong and Xuelong 2, along with another vessel. More than 600 team members from over 100 domestic institutions are participating, and the team is expected to return to China in April 2027 after completing its tasks. The expedition will complete final construction and acceptance work at the Qinling Station, including its main building, communications systems and sewage treatment facilities, to further strengthen its operational support and scientific research capacity, said Luo Guangfu, head of the station. The mission will also advance long-term monitoring of the polar ocean and polynyas. It will also carry out site surveys and mapping for planned supporting facilities at a prospective new research station. As the Great Wall and Zhongshan stations have operated for decades, the team will prepare for upgrades, including safety assessments of fuel storage tanks and station buildings, said Jin Xinmiao, head of the Zhongshan Station. Building on the 3,413-meter ice-sheet drilling achieved during the 42nd expedition, the team will continue clean hot-water drilling through the overlying ice and carry out in-situ observation and sampling of a subglacial lake. The team will also conduct multidisciplinary surveys and long-term monitoring covering physical oceanography, marine chemistry and marine biology, focusing on the impact of climate change on the marine ecosystem. Several types of domestically developed polar equipment, including unmanned aircraft, ground vehicles, pressurized buildings, ice-surface machinery, and modular facilities, will be tested in Antarctica to strengthen China's self-reliant polar support capacity. The expedition will also cooperate with Norway, Chile and Bulgaria on research into Antarctic ice sheets, geology and snow and ice environments, and invite scientists from Thailand, France, Belgium, Portugal and China's Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions to participate. "Pursuing scientific answers in the frozen frontier, we are confident in completing the mission," said Zhang Tijun, leader and chief scientist of China's 43rd Antarctic expedition. item.title: Explainer: What to know about election of delegates to 21st CPC National Congress
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-08
Explainer: What to know about election of delegates to 21st CPC National Congress BEIJING, Nov. 8 (Xinhua) -- The Communist Party of China (CPC), the world's largest governing party, has launched the process of electing delegates to its 21st national congress, which is scheduled to be held in the second half of 2027 in Beijing. An official from the Organization Department of the CPC Central Committee has explained why the election matters, how it will be organized, and what standards eligible candidates must meet. Here is what to know about the election. The 21st CPC National Congress comes at a critical time when the CPC has been working to basically realize socialist modernization and heading toward the Second Centenary Goal. It will be a highly important meeting and an event of great political significance for both the Party and the country, as a new CPC Central Committee and a new CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection will be elected. The 2,360 delegates to be elected should be outstanding Party members who carry the trust of more than 101 million CPC members and over 5.4 million Party organizations as they fulfill their duties at the congress. The successful election of delegates and the completion of all tasks at the congress are vital to consolidating the Party's long-term governing position and enabling the Party to fully exercise its role as the leadership core. They are also closely linked to the prosperity and long-term stability of the Party and the country. The election should be a process of studying and implementing Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, particularly Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building. Xi Jinping, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has attached great importance to carrying out sound work related to the election. He heard multiple reports on this matter. He also presided over meetings of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, at which a circular on the election was deliberated and adopted. The key to ensuring the success of the election is upholding the Party's overall leadership and the centralized, unified leadership of the CPC Central Committee. Emphasis must be placed on examining candidates' political stance and awareness, as well as their capacity for political judgment, thinking and implementation. Their integrity and conduct must also be subject to strict scrutiny. The delegates elected should be well-structured in composition and broadly representative, drawing from a wide range of fields, including the economy, science and technology, national defense, law enforcement and the justice system, education, public communication, culture, health, sports and social administration. They should also include workers in new forms of employment. Front-line workers should account for an appropriate proportion of the delegates. Among delegates from provincial-level regions, central financial institutions and central state-owned enterprises in Beijing, Party members working on the front line should generally account for at least one-third. Among delegates from central Party and state departments, the proportion should generally be no less than 15 percent. In regions where the new economy and new forms of business are thriving and there are large numbers of workers in new forms of employment, outstanding Party members from among these workers should also be recommended as candidates. Particular attention should be paid to recommending model workers, farmers and professionals as candidates. Women Party members and Party members from ethnic minority groups should each make up a certain proportion of the delegates. Political, organizational and electoral disciplines must be strictly observed throughout the election process, with efforts made to prevent vote-buying and other electoral violations and strengthen oversight and enforcement. The electoral procedure consists of five steps: nomination of candidates, assessment of nominees by electoral units, formation of a preliminary list of candidates, formation of a preparatory list of candidates, and formal election. The delegates will be elected through a process in which the number of candidates must exceed the number of seats by more than 15 percent. The delegates elected will be vetted by a qualification review committee prior to the national congress. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.
